title: NATless regional egress and split-horizon DNS patterns
body:
Purpose:
This note captures a compact, opinionated pattern for achieving controlled regional egress for private deployments without relying on per-subnet NAT gateways. It focuses on: (1) using VPC interface endpoints + TLS origination to avoid internet-facing NAT, (2) split-horizon DNS and resolver chaining to direct host resolution appropriately, and (3) hybrid on-prem / cloud handoff via regional transit peering or SD‑WAN. The audience is SEs running customer POCs and infra engineers sizing/prototyping private inference on constrained networks.

Context / Problem statement:
Customers want: low-latency access to model artifacts and telemetry sinks, strong egress controls for compliance (allow-lists, DLP inspection), and minimal public attack surface. Traditional NAT-gateway per-AZ patterns are expensive at scale and complicate IP allow-lists (source IPs vary by AZ and scale events). Some customers are disallowed from internet-bound NATs or want explicit TLS-terminating proxies for logging and inspection.

Goals for this pattern:
- Avoid internet-facing NATs where possible ("NATless").
- Provide stable, predictable egress IPs per-region for customer allowlists.
- Enable service discovery and routing via split-horizon DNS so internal services and managed endpoints resolve to private interfaces.
- Support fallbacks (egress to secondary region or via customer-managed proxy) when capacity/policy constraints occur.
- Keep latency and operational complexity reasonable for POC timelines (2–4 weeks).

Core components and responsibilities:
1) VPC Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) + Private DNS
   - Expose Redwood-managed services (model fetch, telemetry ingestion, auth) as customer-visible interface endpoints in the customer's VPC (or via shared-services VPC).
   - Use interface endpoints with private DNS enabled for automatic resolution of service hostnames to eni IPs.
   - For external 3rd-party sinks (e.g., S3, artifact registries), prefer provider-managed gateway endpoints or S3 interface endpoints where supported.

2) Regional Egress Proxy Fleet (TLS origination inside customer VPC or managed VPC)
   - Deploy a small fleet of autoscaling proxy instances (envoy/nginx) in a dedicated egress subnet. Proxies perform TLS origination to external services and present a stable outbound IP via an egress NAT / elastic IP (only at the proxy layer).
   - For strict NATless posture, proxies can be regional VMs in a shared-services VPC with transit peering; we minimize number of NAT Elastic IPs and centralize allow-listing.
   - Proxies perform request/response logging, header enforcement, and can forward to inspection appliances when required.

3) Split-horizon DNS + Resolver Chaining
   - Create private hosted zones for redwood-internal domains (e.g., models.redwood.local) that point to interface endpoint IPs in the VPC.
   - Use resolver rules to forward customer.onprem.local -> on-prem DNS and external hostnames -> public resolvers, or to a regional resolver that handles zone delegation.
   - For shared-services model catalog names, we recommend delegated private hosted zones per customer to avoid cross-tenant leakage.

4) Transit / Peering / SD-WAN Handoff
   - For on-prem or corporate networks, route egress through a regional transit VPC using VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway (or cloud vendor equivalent).
   - SD‑WAN appliances can terminate on the transit VPC and provide firewalling/DLP before handing back to partner proxies.

Tradeoffs and notes:
- Cost: Eliminating per-subnet NAT reduces hourly and data-processing costs; however, interface endpoints + proxy ELIP costs and added complexity offset savings for small deployments. Evaluate at POC scale.
- Latency: Adding a proxy hop for TLS origination adds 10–40ms typical; consider colocating proxies in same AZs for latency-sensitive inference traffic.
- Operational surface: Interface endpoints simplify DNS but increase per-service management. Automate endpoint provisioning in IaC (Terraform module recommended).
- Failover: Design automatic fallback rules: if regional endpoints fail, route to secondary region or degrade to a lower-cost public path under explicit policy.

Implementation checklist for a POC (2–3 week runway):
- [ ] Provision interface endpoints for core services (auth, model store, telemetry) in 2 AZs. (owner: Mateo)
- [ ] Create private hosted zone and confirm split-horizon resolutions with resolver rules. (owner: Saanvi)
- [ ] Deploy two proxy instances behind an autoscaling group in egress subnet + an Elastic IP and healthchecks. (owner: Liam)
- [ ] Build Terraform module to create endpoints, route53 records, and proxy ASG. (owner: Infra)
- [ ] Run traffic tests: model fetch 99th percentile latency and measuring egress IP stability. (owner: SE/Bench)
- [ ] Demo: show allow-listing by customer firewall using proxy ELIP and a route failover to secondary region. (owner: SE)

Acceptance criteria for customer's POC:
- Customer can add a single IP/CIDR to their allowlist and see model fetch calls succeed across scale events.
- DNS resolves internal services to private IPs within the VPC (no external DNS leakage).
- Egress logs are captured and accessible to customer or forwarded to their SIEM.
- Failover to secondary region occurs within configured SLA (e.g., 90s).

Open questions / blockers:
- Does customer allow creation of interface endpoints in their VPC, or must we host endpoints in a shared-services VPC and peer? (impacts path and IP ownership)
- For customers with strict interception rules, are we allowed to terminate TLS at our proxy, or must we support in-line TLS inspection at the customer perimeter?
- How will private hosted zone delegation be managed for large fleets of customers? Need lifecycle ownership (on delete, on rotation).

Suggested next steps and timeline:
Week 0–1: Confirm endpoint creation permissions and target services. Spin up private hosted zone and a single interface endpoint.
Week 1–2: Deploy proxy ASG and run synthetic model fetches, collect egress IPs and latencies.
Week 2–3: Add resolver chaining to on-prem, demo allow-listing, and capture logs into customer SIEM.
Week 3+: Capture lessons, convert Terraform modules into a reusable SE kit, and propose an enterprise checklist for Dedicated/Private installs.

Appendix: quick config snippets / references
- Terraform: interface endpoint + private DNS example: link in linked_artifacts repo.
- Healthcheck/ASG policy: prefer lifecycle hooks for graceful drain during scale-down.
- Monitoring: instrument proxy with 99/95/50 latency metrics and token-level traces for a sample of requests.

Notes to SEs: keep demos simple—show a single allowlist IP change and a DNS record flip. Customers understand tangible knobs ("give me one IP to add and I can make this work"). Capture screenshots of resolver outputs (dig + short TTLs) for the final POC report.

Decision log summary:
- Pattern chosen: Interface endpoints + regional egress proxies (centralized ELIP) for predictable outbound identity.
- Rationale: predictable allowlists, minimized public NATs, clearer auditing for compliance.
- Risk: added latency and operational complexity vs simple NAT gateway approach.

Action owners / next meetings:
- Mateo: prototype endpoint + hosted zone (due 2025-11-12)
- Liam: prototype proxy ASG + ELIP with basic logging (due 2025-11-14)
- Saanvi: validate DNS forwarding to on-prem resolver and prepare demo script (due 2025-11-16)

-- end of note --
